    ctx user guide

    Getting started

    Install ctx

    Prepare your shell for a client workspace, then check that ctx can find the tools it needs.

    Install on your machine

    Run the full installer in a macOS or Linux terminal. On Windows, open a WSL2 Linux shell first. The installer sets up the CLI and shell integration. For a reproducible installation, use a release tag you have reviewed in place of main. 

    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Hei-Tech-Inc/ctx/main/install.sh | bash

    Check your installation

    Open a fresh terminal so the shell loads the installed hook. The version command confirms which release is on your path. Doctor checks the shell hook, SSH include and integration tools. A machine with no client profiles can still run these checks. 

    ctx version
ctx doctor
    Next guide · Create a profile

    Getting started

    Create a profile

    Use one profile per client so Git, GitHub and your cloud tools use the intended identity.

    Choose an identity and folder

    Start the wizard and choose full setup. For this guide, use acme as the profile name. Supply your client Git name and email, and choose a dedicated work directory such as ~/clients/acme. Select the SSH key and cloud accounts that belong to the client. Review the paths and identities before confirming. 

    ctx setup

    Check the saved profile

    The dashboard shows the workspace, Git email, SSH key path and configured integrations together. Verify checks the profile’s paths and GitHub SSH authentication. A warning about a missing key can be expected if you skipped SSH setup. 

    ctx dashboard
ctx verify acme

    Start with Git only

    Choose clone-only setup if you just need a GitHub SSH alias today. Extend the same profile later when you know the workspace and cloud settings. 

    ctx setup --scope clone
ctx setup --extend acme
    Next guide · Switch workspaces

    Daily use

    Switch workspaces

    Use the current directory to select a profile, or activate one explicitly for a terminal session.

    Enter the client folder

    Change into the directory you selected during setup. At the next prompt, inspect the active profile. In a client repository, git config user.email should match the email in your dashboard. 

    cd ~/clients/acme
ctx status
echo "$CTX_ACTIVE_PROFILE"

    Switch manually

    Use the shell function installed by ctx to apply the profile variables to your current terminal. To see when automatic switching happens, enable transition messages. Clear a manual activation with deactivate. 

    ctx use acme
ctx config autoswitch-notify on
ctx deactivate

    Resolve a nested workspace

    When several clients share a repository, place a .ctx file containing profile=acme in the directory that belongs to that client. The nearest override takes precedence. Check the result from inside that directory. 

    ctx status --json
    Next guide · Clone with GitHub

    Daily use

    Clone with GitHub

    Route a clone through the client’s SSH alias and confirm the repository uses its Git identity.

    Clone into the workspace

    Replace ORG and REPO with a repository you can access. Start in the client folder. The profile option selects the GitHub SSH alias even if a different profile is active. 

    cd ~/clients/acme
ctx clone -p acme git@github.com:ORG/REPO.git

    Inspect the checkout

    Enter the new repository. Its origin should use github-acme for the SSH host. Compare the email with the profile before committing. Verify tests the client SSH connection. 

    cd REPO
git remote get-url origin
git config user.email
ctx verify acme

    Guard commits and pushes

    Install the Git guard if you want ctx to check the email on commit and the SSH alias on push. Check its status inside the repository because a repository-specific hooks path can take precedence. 

    ctx guard install
ctx guard status
    Next guide · Run commands and scripts

    Automation

    Run commands and scripts

    Give one process the client identity without switching every other terminal.

    Run with a named profile

    Put the program and its arguments after the double dash. The child inherits the profile’s Git identity, GitHub credentials and configured cloud variables. For kubectl, pass the intended context explicitly. 

    ctx run -p acme -- git var GIT_AUTHOR_IDENT
ctx run -p acme -- gh auth status

    Read structured checks

    Use list to enumerate profiles and status to inspect activation. Doctor emits machine-wide checks. Verify emits profile checks and returns status 1 on failure. For diagnostic results, inspect each check’s level and message. 

    ctx --json list
ctx --json status
ctx --json doctor
ctx --json verify acme

    Store a secret

    Set the value at the interactive prompt to avoid putting it in your command history. List shows key names. Processes launched with ctx run can receive the profile’s stored secrets, so select the child process deliberately. 

    ctx secret set acme API_TOKEN
ctx secret list acme

    Support

    Troubleshoot activation

    Work from the observed identity to the profile, shell hook or SSH setting that selected it.

    The shell shows the wrong client

    Compare the active profile, work directory and Git email. Check for a nearer .ctx override and for a manual activation. From the client repository, inspect which Git config file supplied the email. 

    ctx status
ctx dashboard
git config --show-origin --get user.email

    Changing directories does nothing

    Transition messages are off by default. Check the actual profile first. If the shell hook is missing, install it, open a new terminal and re-enter the client folder. 

    ctx doctor
ctx install-hook

    GitHub uses the wrong key

    Check the origin URL inside the checkout. A client clone uses the profile alias, such as github-acme. Doctor checks the SSH include and verify checks the profile key, alias and live authentication. 

    git remote -v
ctx doctor
ctx verify acme
